after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Find the equation of the left-opening parabola that has its vertex at $(0,0)$ and passes through the point $(-6,-4).$
after.worked_solution:
The general standard equation of a parabola whose vertex is $(0,0)$ and whose arms open right or left is given by

$$
{y}^{2}=4px.
$$

Since we know the given parabola passes through the point $(-6,-4),$ we can substitute $x=-6$ and $y=-4$ into the standard equation and solve for $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =4px \\ (-4)^{2} & =4p(-6) \\ 16 & =-24p \\ p & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation of the parabola is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2} & =4px \\ {y}^{2} & =4(-\frac{2}{3})x \\ {y}^{2} & =-\frac{8}{3}x.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: Find the equation of the right-opening parabola that has its vertex at $(-4,-1)$ and passes through the point $(5,2).$
after.worked_solution:
The general standard equation of a parabola whose vertex is $(h,k)$ and whose arms open right or left is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-k)^{2} & =4p(x-h).\end{aligned}
$$

Since we know that the given parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(-4,-1),$ we substitute $h=-4$ and $k=-1$ into the equation above and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+1)^{2} & =4p(x+4).\end{aligned}
$$

We also know that the given parabola passes through the point $(5,2),$ so we can substitute $x=5$ and $y=2$ into the equation above and solve for $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+1)^{2} & =4p(x+4) \\ (2+1)^{2} & =4p(5+4) \\ 9 & =36p \\ p & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation of the parabola is

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+1)^{2} & =4p(x+4) \\ (y+1)^{2} & =4(\frac{1}{4})(x+4) \\ (y+1)^{2} & =x+4.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-k)^{2} & =4p(x-h).\end{aligned}
$$

Since we know that the given parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(0,-3),$ we substitute $h=0$ and $k=-3$ into the equation above and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+3)^{2} & =4px.\end{aligned}
$$

We also know that the given parabola passes through the point $(3,0),$ so we can substitute $x=3$ and $y=0$ into the equation above and solve for $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+3)^{2} & =4px \\ (0+3)^{2} & =4p(3) \\ 9 & =12p \\ p & =\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation of the parabola is 

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+3)^{2} & =4px \\ (y+3)^{2} & =4(\frac{3}{4})x \\ (y+3)^{2} & =3x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-k)^{2} & =4p(x-h).\end{aligned}
$$

Since we know that the given parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(1,-3),$ we substitute $h=1$ and $k=-3$ into the equation above and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+3)^{2} & =4p(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

We also know that the given parabola passes through the point $(3,0),$ so we can substitute $x=3$ and $y=0$ into the equation above and solve for $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+3)^{2} & =4p(x-1) \\ (0+3)^{2} & =4p(3-1) \\ 9 & =8p \\ p & =\frac{9}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+3)^{2} & =4p(x-1) \\ (y+3)^{2} & =4(\frac{9}{8})(x-1) \\ (y+3)^{2} & =\frac{9}{2}(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
The general standard equation of a parabola whose vertex is $(h,k)$ and whose arms open right or left is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}(y-k)^{2} & =4p(x-h).\end{aligned}
$$

Since we know that the given parabola has its vertex at $(h,k)=(1,-3),$ we substitute $h=1$ and $k=-3$ into the equation above and get

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+3)^{2} & =4p(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$

We also know that the given parabola passes through the point $(3,0),$ so we can substitute $x=3$ and $y=0$ into the equation above and solve for $p:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+3)^{2} & =4p(x-1) \\ (0+3)^{2} & =4p(3-1) \\ 9 & =8p \\ p & =\frac{9}{8}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation of the parabola is 

$$
\begin{aligned}(y+3)^{2} & =4p(x-1) \\ (y+3)^{2} & =4(\frac{9}{8})(x-1) \\ (y+3)^{2} & =\frac{9}{2}(x-1).\end{aligned}
$$
